title: How to build a case chronology from documents on Mac: steps for lawyers in 2026
metaTitle: Build a Case Chronology From Documents on Mac, Step by Step
description: Build a case chronology from documents on Mac with one fact table, page cites, a conflict log and a verify pass. Steps for lawyers and paralegals.
targetKeyword: build a case chronology from documents

problem: building case chronologies from document sets
intro: To build a case chronology from documents, start with one fact table. Each row holds one dated event, the document it came from, the page and a short quote. This page covers the real costs, the usual causes, fixes you can use today, and where Lazur helps. Lazur can point, explain and dictate. It does not build the table for you.
tldr: Build one fact table with fixed columns: date, event, people, document, page, quote and conflict.
Sort by the event date. The date a file was saved is often wrong for the timeline.
Log every conflict between documents. Do not quietly pick one version of a date.
Verify each row against the original file before anyone relies on the chronology.
Lazur points at columns, explains menus and dictates entries. It does not build the table.

blocks.text: What a case chronology is and what it is for

A case chronology is a dated list of events in a matter. Every entry points back to a source document. Lawyers use it to prepare witnesses, draft statements of fact, test a client's account and spot gaps in the record. In many firms, a paralegal builds the first version. The chronology only works if a colleague can open any row and find the sentence behind it.

Think of the chronology as a table with a source attached to every line. A row that says a demand letter went out is only as good as the letter it cites. If the letter is missing, the row is a guess. That gap separates a timeline you can defend from a list you wrote from memory.
What building one costs you in time and money

No study I could find measures how many hours a chronology takes, how often one contains an error, or how those errors change a case. Budget from your own timing. The part you can measure is the hourly cost of the people doing the work. The Bureau of Labor Statistics puts the May 2025 median pay for lawyers at an hourly equivalent of $76.76. For paralegals and legal assistants, the figure is $30.24 an hour. Those are national wage figures, not billing rates. Treat them as the cost of staff time.

Time is not the only cost. Chronology work is detailed, and it is easy to push back until a deadline forces it. Bloomberg Law's 2025 Attorney Workload and Hours Survey reported average burnout of 42% in 2024, rising to 51% for mid- and senior-level associates. The survey page says full results sit behind a download form, so weekly and billable hours are not visible there.

The chart shows the gap between the two roles. If a paralegal does the first pass and a lawyer checks it, the mix matters. Moving an hour of first-pass reading to a paralegal costs less in wages. That saving holds only if someone still checks the output. Skipping the check saves money on paper and costs more later.

blocks.title: Budget from your own timing
blocks.text: Time two or three real matters before you promise a client a number. Write down the start and stop time for each stage. Your own records beat any survey, including the ones on this page.
Where a chronology breaks down, and why

Most broken chronologies fail in the same few places. The documents arrive out of order, the dates come from the wrong field, the same event appears in several versions, or a row has no source. Each one is easy to miss on a busy day. Each one turns a useful table into a list you cannot defend.

The first trap is the file date. A scanned letter can be saved long after it was written. Finder shows a created and a modified date for each file, and neither one is the date of the event. Open the document, read the date in the text and log that date. If the text has no date, mark the row undated and leave the date blank.

The second trap is duplicates. An email chain repeats the same meeting in every reply. A draft and a final version can describe one event with different times. Pick one anchor row, cite every copy, and log the differences. If two documents disagree on a fact, see [how to compare two Word documents on a Mac](/for/lawyers/problems/compare-two-word-documents-on-mac) to find the change.
How to build the fact table, step by step

items: Gather every document into one matter folder, then copy the set into a working folder. Keep the originals untouched.
Read each document once and log every dated event in a single table, even when you are unsure.
Fill in people, document name, page or paragraph, and a short quote for each row.
Sort the table by event date. Mark any row that conflicts with another row.
Check each row against its original file. Mark it verified only after you find the words in the source.

blocks.text: This follows the five-step method that CaseTime describes on its blog. Gather the filings and correspondence. Identify the key events. Build a dated list with a date, a description and a significance note for each. Cite the document and page for every event. Then review each citation against the original.
A worked example of one fact table row
Use the same columns for every row, in the same order. A colleague can then scan the sheet fast. You can sort or search without rewriting anything. The table below works for most matters.

blocks.caption: Columns for a fact table that works for most matters.
rows: Date
The date the event happened, in one format such as YYYY-MM-DD
Typing the date the file was saved
Event
One plain sentence with a clear verb
A summary of what you think it means
People
Names as written, with role in brackets
Two spellings of one person in different rows
Document
File name and any control or Bates number
A folder name with no file name
Page or paragraph
Where the sentence appears
Leaving it blank because the file is short
Quote and conflict
The exact words, plus the other version of any conflicting date
A paraphrase in quotation marks, or a conflict noticed but not logged

blocks.text: A finished row reads like a short sentence with a source. The date comes from the body of the document. The event is one plain sentence, such as a tenant reporting a leak to a landlord. The people column names both parties as written. The document column holds the file name. The page column says where the sentence sits. The quote column holds the exact words. Any conflict goes in its own column or tab.
Date handling: event dates, time zones and file dates

Email adds its own trap. An email header records the time in the sender's time zone. Mail or Outlook then shows that time in your Mac's time zone, so the same message can look like a different day. Check the sent time shown in the message before you record a same-day event. Write the zone in the event note when the time matters to the story.

On your Mac, select a file in Finder and press ⌘I to open Get Info. Compare the created and modified dates with what the document says. Use those dates as a clue only, never as the event date. If you sort by date in Finder, go to View > Sort By and check which date you are sorting by.

items: Sorting by the date a file was saved, not the date of the event.
Logging a conflict in one row and forgetting the other version.
Paraphrasing a passage and then putting it in quotation marks.
Skipping the verify pass because the first pass looked clean.
Keeping two copies of the table, so the old one gets shared by mistake.

blocks.text: Using AI for a first pass, and where it stops

AI can help with the first pass. Vaquill, an AI vendor, describes a workflow where AI proposes dated events, each with a source link, and a person checks them. Vaquill's post says the verify step is not optional. It cites no measured accuracy or time savings, so treat its claims as marketing until you test them on your own documents.

blocks.title: Check the rules first
blocks.text: Before any client document goes into an AI tool, read your firm's policy on client data. Ask a supervising lawyer or IT if the policy is unclear. Your employer's rules come first. This page cannot tell you what your firm allows.

If your firm allows an AI tool, use it to propose rows, not to decide what happened. Every proposed row needs a source you open yourself. A tool that gives a date without a page or paragraph is not giving you a chronology row. Mark the proposed rows in a separate column so reviewers can see which ones a person has checked.
Timeline software for Mac and what the vendors say

Dedicated tools exist. Aeon Timeline's legal page says you can import facts from a CSV or spreadsheet file, link events to documents and witnesses, and compare accounts. Its platforms page lists a Mac app that needs macOS 10.13 or later. The pages I read show no prices, so check their pricing page before you budget.

CaseFleet runs in a browser. Its comparison page, which is vendor marketing, lists Mac among supported browser platforms. It also states pricing from $30 per user per month, with a 14-day free trial. The same page says CaseMap Cloud was rebranded CaseMap+ AI in March 2025, and lists no public pricing. I could not confirm Mac support for classic CaseMap or TimeMap. A competitor calls them Windows-only, but I did not verify that, so ask the vendor.

blocks.text: You do not need a paid tool to start. Word tables, Pages tables and Apple's Numbers app can hold the same columns. Apple's Numbers support page says Numbers works on Mac, iPad and iPhone, with formulas that include hundreds of built-in functions. For Word, see [Word for lawyers on Mac](/for/lawyers/word). Sort on the date column, and keep one master file.
How to verify every row before anyone relies on it

The verify pass is where a chronology earns trust. Open the original file, find the words in the quote column and check the date, the names and the wording. In Word, press ⌘F and search for a few words from the quote to jump to them. In Chrome, open the source page and press ⌘F there too. Mark the row verified only after you see the words yourself.

Keep a verified column with your initials and the date you checked. A second person reading the same row with fresh eyes tends to catch different mistakes. Have that person check a sample of verified rows before the chronology goes to a supervising lawyer.

Some sources live on the web, such as a public docket or a company's press release. Save a copy when you first cite it. In Chrome, press ⌘P, then choose PDF > Save as PDF. Store the PDF in the matter folder. A web page can change or disappear, and the saved copy will not. For more on Chrome, see [Chrome for lawyers on Mac](/for/lawyers/chrome).
Keeping the chronology current as documents arrive

A chronology is never finished. New productions arrive, and a clean table gets messy fast. Keep one master file with a version date in its name. Add new rows at the bottom, then re-sort by event date. Recheck the new rows and any row they touch, not the whole table.
Where Lazur fits, and where it does not

Lazur is a voice assistant for the Mac. Hold ⌥ ⌘ and ask about anything on screen, and Lazur answers out loud. Ask where a control sits, and Lazur draws a circle and a label around it. Ask how to do something, and Lazur guides you one click at a time, waiting for each click. Hold fn to dictate clean text at the cursor in any app.

Lazur does not click buttons, edit files or operate other apps for you. It does not scan your case folder or fill in rows on its own. Reading each source and deciding what it proves stays with you. Lazur can help you find the right column, explain a menu, dictate an entry and draft a line for you to check.

On privacy, Lazur listens and looks at the screen only while you hold the shortcut. Audio and the screenshot go to AI providers to answer you, and they are not stored. Content is never used to train AI models. Your firm's rules still decide whether client material should be on screen while you ask a question.

faq.question: How long does it take to build a case chronology from documents?
faq.answer: No public study I could find measures this. Your own timing is the most reliable figure you have. Time your first two matters from start to finish, including the verify pass. Then turn those hours into a cost using staff wage figures, not billing rates.

faq.question: Which app should I use on a Mac, Word, Pages or Numbers?
faq.answer: Use the one your firm already shares, so colleagues can open the file. Word has tables and Find with ⌘F, which helps with quote checks. Pages can hold a table too. Numbers suits sorting and formulas, and Apple's Numbers page lists hundreds of built-in functions.

faq.question: Does Lazur read my documents and fill in the table?
faq.answer: No. Lazur does not click buttons, edit files or fill in rows for you. It can point at a column, explain a menu, dictate text at the cursor and draft wording that you then check. Reading and verifying each source stays with you.

faq.question: Is it safe to put client documents into an AI tool?
faq.answer: This page cannot answer that for your firm. Check your firm's policy and the rules that bind your work before you upload anything. Your employer's rules on client data come first.

faq.question: What is the difference between a chronology and a timeline?
faq.answer: In practice, a chronology usually means a cited table of dated events. A timeline often means a visual graphic. Some people use the words loosely. Ask the supervising lawyer which format they want before you start.

faq.question: What do I do with an undated document?
faq.answer: Keep it out of the dated rows. Put it in a separate list with the file name, a short description and the word undated. Do not assign a date from the file's saved date. If the document matters, raise it with the team.

faq.question: Do I need special software for this?
faq.answer: No. A table in Word, Pages or Numbers can hold the same columns. Dedicated tools such as Aeon Timeline and CaseFleet exist. Check their pricing pages before you decide, because the pages I read did not give clear prices.

costs.title: Staff hours at wage rates
costs.text: Every hour of chronology work is an hour of someone's pay. The Bureau of Labor Statistics lists an hourly equivalent of $76.76 for lawyers and $30.24 an hour for paralegals, based on the May 2025 medians. Use those as the cost of staff time, not a billing rate. Your firm's own rates will differ, so use them for your budget.

costs.title: Rework when a late error surfaces
costs.text: Errors found late cost the most. A wrong date discovered during deposition prep forces the whole chronology to be rebuilt under pressure. No public study measures how often this happens. Count it in your own matters, and keep a note whenever you fix a row that someone else has already used.

costs.title: Team burnout
costs.text: Bloomberg Law's 2025 survey reported average burnout of 42% in 2024, and 51% for mid- and senior-level associates. The survey does not link chronology work to burnout, so do not present it as proof. Long, unstructured review is hard work, and it is worth planning breaks around it.

costs.title: Gaps you cannot explain in the room
costs.text: A chronology that skips a key email leaves you exposed. If opposing counsel uses a document you never logged, you have to explain the gap on the spot. Build the table from every document in the set, not only the ones you already like. Log undated documents too, in a separate list.

causes.title: Documents arrive with no order
causes.text: Productions and client folders mix emails, PDFs, scanned letters and text messages. Nothing in the pile sorts them by event. A reader who starts at the first file and works down can miss dates that sit inside later files. Build the table from the content of each document, not from the order of the folder.

causes.title: File dates are not event dates
causes.text: A file's created or modified date tells you when a copy was made. It does not tell you when the event happened. A scanned letter may be saved years after it was written. Read the date inside the text, log that date, and note the file date only when it helps explain a conflict.

causes.title: The same event appears many times
causes.text: An email chain repeats the same meeting in every reply. A draft and a final version can describe one event twice, sometimes with different times. Without a rule for duplicates, the table swells and the story gets confusing. Pick one anchor row, cite all the copies, and log the differences between them.

causes.title: Finding the right documents is its own job
causes.text: Before you can date events, you have to find the relevant documents. Grossman and Cormack argue that technology-assisted review can produce better results than exhaustive manual review on the TREC 2009 Legal Track data, measured by recall, precision and F1. Their work is about finding documents, not writing the chronology. It still shows that the search is a separate task, so plan time for it.

causes.title: Copy and paste drift
causes.text: People retype dates, shorten names and paste quotes from memory. One row says a meeting was on one day, another row puts it on a different day, and nobody notices. Copy quotes directly from the source file, and keep a single master table so each version of a row does not become a new fact.

causes.title: Time zones in email headers
causes.text: Email timestamps depend on the time zone of the sender's device. A same-day event can land on the wrong side of midnight if you read the time in a different zone. Check the sent time shown in the message, and note the zone when the time matters to the story.

causes.title: First-pass AI sounds sure
causes.text: AI tools write clean, confident rows. A confident row can still carry a wrong date, an invented name or a quote that is not in the source. Vaquill says the verify step is not optional, and it cites no accuracy data. Treat every AI row as a draft until you open the source.

fixes.title: Use one fact table with fixed columns
fixes.text: Create one table with the same columns for every row: date, event, people, document, page or paragraph, quote, conflict and verified. Word, Pages and Numbers can all hold it on a Mac. Fixed columns make sorting, searching and checking faster for everyone. Do not add columns mid-matter without telling the team.

fixes.title: Name working copies by event date
fixes.text: Rename copies in a working folder so each file name starts with the event date, in the same format every time. In Finder, select a file and press ⌘I to check its dates. Keep the original file name in the document column, so the link back to the source stays clear.

fixes.title: Run a two-pass build
fixes.text: First pass: read each document once and log every dated event, even uncertain ones. Second pass: open each source again and confirm the date, names and quote. Splitting the work this way stops you from polishing rows you have not checked. It also gives you a clean moment to log conflicts.

fixes.title: Keep a conflict log
fixes.text: Create a second tab or sheet called Conflicts. Each row names two documents, the two versions of the date or fact, and the version the chronology uses for now. Do not choose silently. A written conflict is easy to resolve later, while a hidden one can surprise you at a hearing.

fixes.title: Quote the source, do not paraphrase
fixes.text: Copy exact words from the source into the quote column, and put any summary in the event column. Use Find with ⌘F in Word to confirm the quote appears in the document. If the quote does not match word for word, fix it before you mark the row verified.

fixes.title: Save web sources as PDFs
fixes.text: For a public web page, press ⌘P in Chrome, then choose PDF > Save as PDF. Store the PDF in the matter folder and cite it in the document column. A web page can change or disappear, and the saved copy will not.

fixes.title: Treat AI output as a draft
fixes.text: If your firm allows an AI tool, ask it for candidate rows with the page or paragraph it used. Then open every source and check each row yourself. Mark rows the tool proposed in their own column, so a reader can tell which ones a person has verified.

fixes.title: Check the rules before any upload
fixes.text: Before any client document goes into an AI tool, read your firm's policy on client data. Ask a supervising lawyer or IT if the policy is unclear. This page cannot tell you what your firm allows, and your employer's rules come first.

plan.label: Day 1
plan.title: Collect and copy
plan.text: Gather every document into one matter folder, then copy the set into a working folder. Keep the originals untouched. Create the fact table with its fixed columns, and save it with a clear name and a version date.

plan.label: Day 2
plan.title: First pass
plan.text: Read each document once. Log every dated event in the table, including uncertain ones. Put undated documents in a separate list instead of guessing a date.

plan.label: Day 3
plan.title: Second pass and verify
plan.text: Open each source again. Confirm the date, the names and the exact quote, using Find with ⌘F where it helps. Mark a row verified only when you have seen the words in the original file.

plan.label: Day 4
plan.title: Conflicts and review
plan.text: Open the Conflicts tab and decide, in writing, what the team will use for each conflict. Ask a second person to check a sample of verified rows. Note any row that still lacks a source.

plan.label: Morning
plan.title: Daily update
plan.text: Each morning, add new productions to the bottom of the table. Re-sort by event date, then check only the new rows and any rows they touch. Save a dated version before you close the file.
